items.prompt: Define stakeholder.
items.canonical_answer: A stakeholder is any individual or group with an interest in the activities of a business: affected by what the business does, able to affect what it does, or both.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning only. The definition has to carry the idea of an interest - something the party stands to gain or lose - rather than any connection to the business.
No example and no evaluation are required at this tariff.

items.prompt: Identify five parties normally treated as stakeholders of a manufacturing business.
items.canonical_answer: Its owners or shareholders. Its employees. Its customers. Its suppliers. The government. Its managers, the providers of its finance and the local community around the plant are also stakeholders of such a business.
marking_guidance: Naming is what is credited; nothing beyond naming is required.
Any five of the recognised parties are acceptable.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a stakeholder and a shareholder.
items.canonical_answer: A shareholder owns part of a limited company, and that ownership gives a financial interest in the company's results, so every shareholder is a stakeholder. A stakeholder need not own any part of the business: customers, suppliers, employees and neighbours qualify on the strength of what they stand to gain or lose. The practical difference is in rights. Ownership carries entitlements set out in company law - voting at a general meeting, receiving the accounts, sharing in any dividend declared. A stakeholder who owns nothing has rights where a contract or a law creates them, and expectations elsewhere.
marking_guidance: Boundary: the distinction is ownership. Both sides must appear - a shareholder owns part of the company, a stakeholder need not own anything.
Credit the consequence of the difference, which is that ownership carries rights in company law whereas other stakeholders rely on contract or statute.

items.prompt: Zambezi River Lodge employs 34 people from a village of about 500. It buys fresh produce from four growers within 20 km, each of whom sells it roughly a tenth of their crop. Its guests are booked through eight European travel agents, the largest of which fills a third of its beds. Using these facts, explain which stakeholder has the strongest interest in the lodge continuing to trade.
items.canonical_answer: The village has the strongest interest. Thirty-four of about 500 residents earn their income from the lodge, and in a settlement of that size the wages of 34 households support much of the local spending too, so a large share of the community's income rests on the lodge. Strength of interest is measured by how much of a party's income, custom, amenity or capital depends on the business, not by how strongly it feels. Measured that way the growers rank low, because each sells the lodge only about a tenth of its crop and can place the rest elsewhere. The largest travel agent fills a third of the beds, so the lodge depends heavily on it, but the agent has many other lodges to sell and so has little riding on this one - a case where dependence runs strongly in one direction only.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the lodge's own facts - 34 employees in a village of 500, a tenth of each grower's crop, a third of beds from one agent.
Reasoning: the link must be the share of each party's income or custom that rests on the lodge, not how strongly it would object.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a named party and say why the others rank below it.

context.situation: rural lodge with local employment and export-booked guests
facts: four growers, one tenth of crop each
largest agent fills one third of beds

items.prompt: Explain why two stakeholders of the same business can have very different strengths of interest in it.
items.canonical_answer: Because an interest is what a party stands to gain or lose, and different parties have different amounts resting on the business. The strength of an interest is measured by the share of that party's income, custom, amenity or capital that depends on the business. A supplier selling nine tenths of its output to one customer loses almost everything if that customer stops buying; a supplier selling a tenth of its output to the same customer loses a slice it can probably replace. Both are stakeholders, and the first has far more at stake. The reason this matters is that the size of the stake predicts how hard the party will work to influence the decision.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must ground the difference in the share of income, custom, amenity or capital that rests on the business.
Purpose: it must say why the difference matters - the stake predicts the effort the party puts into influencing the business - rather than only that stakes differ.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an internal and an external stakeholder, including what the line between them is drawn on.
items.canonical_answer: Internal stakeholders form part of the organisation itself - its owners, its managers and its employees. External stakeholders sit outside it but are affected by it or can affect it, such as customers, suppliers, the providers of finance, the government and the local community. The line is drawn on membership of the organisation, not on how much is at stake. That matters, because an external party can have far more riding on a decision than an internal one: a family living beside a quarry may lose the use of its yard, while a shareholder holding a hundred shares out of a million loses a few cents of dividend.
marking_guidance: Boundary: membership of the organisation is the criterion, and the answer must say so explicitly.
Both sides must be named with at least one member each.
Credit the contrast that external does not mean minor - size of stake does not decide the classification.

items.prompt: A depot supervisor at Omaruru Dairies holds 400 shares in the company under its staff share scheme. The board is deciding whether to close her depot, which would raise the dividend and end her job. Explain how her position differs from that of a shareholder who does not work for the company.
items.canonical_answer: She holds two stakeholder positions at once. As an employee she is an internal stakeholder whose wage and job depend on the depot staying open; as the holder of 400 shares she is an owner whose dividend rises if it closes. The outside shareholder holds only the second position, so the closure reads to him as a clear gain. For the supervisor the two positions pull against each other, and the wage almost certainly dominates: a year's pay is worth far more to her than the dividend on 400 shares in a company of that size. The practical difference is therefore that she has a reason to oppose a decision the outside shareholder has a reason to support, even though both are shareholders.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the named facts - 400 shares, the staff scheme, the depot closure that raises the dividend and ends the job.
Reasoning: the link is that one person can hold two stakeholder positions whose interests point in opposite directions.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude which interest dominates for her, and why the outside shareholder sees the decision differently.

items.prompt: Correct this statement: "A party that is strongly affected by a business must be an internal stakeholder."
items.canonical_answer: The statement confuses the size of the stake with the classification. Internal and external are decided by membership of the organisation - owners, managers and employees are inside it; customers, suppliers, financiers, government and the local community are outside it. How much a party has riding on a decision does not enter into the classification. A household beside a quarry can lose the use of its garden and is still external, while a manager whose department is unaffected by a decision is still internal. The correct version: a party is internal where it forms part of the organisation, whatever the size of its stake.
marking_guidance: The error to be named is that the statement classifies by strength of interest rather than by membership.
A corrected version of the statement is required, not only the diagnosis.
One illustration of a strongly affected external party supports the correction.

items.prompt: Identify the role a supplier plays in relation to a business.
items.canonical_answer: A supplier delivers the inputs the business works with - raw materials, components, stock or services - to an agreed specification and on agreed terms, often including credit that lets the business use the goods before paying for them.
marking_guidance: Naming the part played is what is credited: the supply of inputs on agreed terms.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a stakeholder's rights and a stakeholder's responsibilities.
items.canonical_answer: Rights are what a party is entitled to receive or to do in its dealings with the business - an employee's entitlement to the agreed wage and to the conditions employment legislation sets, a shareholder's entitlement to vote at a general meeting, a supplier's entitlement to payment within the agreed thirty days. Responsibilities are what is expected of that party in return - the employee working to the contract and following safety rules, the supplier delivering to specification and on time, the customer paying for what was supplied. The two are two sides of one relationship, which is the distinction worth holding: one party's right is usually another party's responsibility, so the employee's right to the wage is the employer's responsibility to pay it.
marking_guidance: Boundary: rights are entitlements owed to the party; responsibilities are what is expected of it in return.
Both sides must be illustrated with at least one example each.
Credit the observation that one party's right is usually another's responsibility.

items.prompt: Erongo Transport is a private limited company running twelve trucks between Walvis Bay and Windhoek. Its drivers are employed on written contracts; its fuel supplier delivers on thirty-day credit. Explain the role, one right and one responsibility of its fuel supplier.
items.canonical_answer: Role: the fuel supplier delivers the diesel the fleet runs on, and finances part of the haulier's working capital by allowing thirty days before payment. Right: to be paid the invoice within those thirty days, and to receive orders with the notice the agreement sets. Responsibility: to deliver the quantity and the grade ordered, on the day agreed - a late or contaminated delivery stops trucks that are already committed to customers. The three headings hang together here, because the credit the supplier extends is what gives its right to timely payment its force: it has already parted with the goods.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must be written for this haulier's fuel supplier, using the thirty-day credit term named in the stem.
Reasoning: each heading must be filled with something specific to a fuel supply relationship, because a generic answer about suppliers does not use the facts given.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude with the link between the credit given and the right to be paid on time.

context.situation: twelve-truck haulier on the Walvis Bay to Windhoek route

items.prompt: Explain why a stakeholder's right is usually matched by another party's responsibility.
items.canonical_answer: Because a right in a business relationship is an entitlement against somebody, and that somebody has to deliver it for the right to mean anything. The relationship is an exchange: each party hands over a resource - labour, goods, custom, capital - and takes something back. The taking back is the right; the handing over is the responsibility, seen from the other side. So an employee's right to the agreed wage exists because the employer has the responsibility to pay it, and the supplier's right to payment in thirty days exists because the buyer has the responsibility to settle the invoice. The purpose of noticing this is practical: an answer that lists rights without naming who carries the matching responsibility has described only half of each relationship.
marking_guidance: Reason: rights are entitlements held against a named party, so they exist only where that party carries a matching duty.
Purpose: the answer must say why this matters for analysis - a right described without its counterpart is half a relationship.

items.prompt: Katutura Tailors employs three staff in Namibia and is opening a branch in a neighbouring country where the minimum notice period before dismissal is shorter and there is no statutory paid sick leave. Explain what this means for a statement of its employees' rights.
items.canonical_answer: It means the statement has to say which country's employees it is describing. Rights split into those created by law and those created by agreement. The legal ones follow the jurisdiction the employee works in, so the Namibian staff hold notice and paid sick-leave entitlements that the staff at the new branch do not, even though both work for the same employer doing the same job. The rights created by agreement travel with the contract, so the firm can choose to give its branch staff the same notice and sick pay by writing it into their contracts - in which case those become contractual rights rather than legal ones, enforceable but removable in a way statutory rights are not. The conclusion for an answer is that any claim about employee rights must name the jurisdiction or the contract it rests on.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use this employer's facts - two countries, shorter notice, no statutory sick pay at the new branch.
Reasoning: the link is that legal rights follow the jurisdiction while contractual rights follow the agreement.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude that a statement of rights has to name the country or the contract it rests on.

context.situation: opening a branch in another jurisdiction
facts: no statutory paid sick leave abroad

items.prompt: Okapuka Poultry employs sixty people in packing. It is installing an automated packing line that needs twenty. Analyse the effect of this decision on its employees and on the business itself.
items.canonical_answer: Start from what changes: forty of the sixty packing jobs go, so for those employees job security changes to no income at all, in a district where poultry packing is one of few employers. Because the loss is total for them and no alternative employer is within reach, they have every reason to resist, and because forty people share the same loss they can act together through their union rather than individually. The mechanism by which that reaches the business is the redundancy process: collective objection lengthens consultation, raises the settlements, and holds output down while the dispute runs. The twenty packers who remain see what happened to their colleagues, so willingness to work overtime at short notice is likely to fall. The consequence for the business is that the wage saving of N$4.8 million a year arrives later and smaller than the plan assumes, reduced by settlements, lost output and lower cooperation. The effect on the business's objectives is therefore conditional: the automation still lowers unit cost over the life of the line, but the payback is slower, and if the dispute runs long enough to cost a major retail contract the decision damages the revenue it was meant to protect.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from the condition given - forty of sixty packing jobs going in a district with few alternative employers.
Mechanism: the answer must say how the reaction reaches the business, through consultation, settlements, lost output and reduced cooperation.
Consequence: a measurable effect is required - the wage saving arriving later and smaller than planned.
Objective: the chain must finish on an effect on the business, and must stay conditional rather than asserting that the decision fails.

facts: wage saving N$4.8 million a year

items.prompt: Namib Clay Bricks sells 45 per cent of its output to one large construction firm and the rest to about forty small builders. It has announced a 12 per cent price rise to all customers. Explain which customer is more likely to react in a way that changes the decision.
items.canonical_answer: The large construction firm. Reaction size depends on how much is at stake for the party, whether it has an alternative, and how much influence it can bring to bear, and the large firm scores higher on the last two. A 12 per cent rise on 45 per cent of output is a material sum for a single buyer, large enough to justify the cost of seeking quotes from other brickworks, and the brickworks depends on that account for nearly half its volume, so the threat of moving carries real weight. The forty small builders each face the same percentage rise on a much smaller order; individually none is worth accommodating, and forty separate firms have no ready way to act together, so their objections arrive as complaints rather than as pressure. The conclusion is that the rise is more likely to be softened or staged for the large account than withdrawn across the board.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the split given - 45 per cent to one buyer, the rest across about forty small builders, and a 12 per cent rise.
Reasoning: the link must run through dependence, the availability of an alternative and the ability to act together.
Conclusion: the answer must reach a named customer and say what the likely change to the decision is.

items.prompt: A poultry processor is deciding whether to replace forty packing jobs with an automated line that would save N$4.8 million a year in wages. Evaluate whether the likely reactions of its stakeholders should change that decision.
items.canonical_answer: They should change how the decision is carried out, and should change whether it is taken only where the reaction is large enough to overturn the saving. The decisive test is whether the priced reaction - redundancy settlements, output lost during consultation, reduced cooperation from the packers who remain, and any contract put at risk by disrupted supply - comes to more than the N$4.8 million the automation saves each year. That is a comparison the business can actually make, whereas the strength of feeling around the decision is not. Applied to this processor, the reactions are likely to be substantial but finite: settlements are a one-off cost, lost cooperation fades, and the wage saving recurs every year, so on a three-year view the automation is likely to remain worth doing. The strongest argument the other way is that the costs are not all inside the business. A processor that is the main employer in its district may find the regional authority slower with its next permit and its recruitment harder for years, and neither shows up in the redundancy budget. The judgement is therefore that the reactions should reshape the plan - phased redeployment, early consultation with the union, retraining for some of the forty - rather than cancel it. That reverses where the processor is dependent on a single customer whose supply the dispute would interrupt, because one lost contract can exceed several years of wage saving.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a plain recommendation is required - reshape the plan rather than cancel it - not a balanced list.
Context: the argument must be made for this processor, using the N$4.8 million saving and the forty jobs.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the priced reaction set against the recurring wage saving.
Counterargument: the answer must give real weight to the costs that fall outside the redundancy budget.
Condition: it must name what reverses the judgement, such as dependence on a single customer whose supply a dispute would interrupt.

facts: wage saving N$4.8 million a year

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which a dissatisfied customer's reaction reaches a business's results.
items.canonical_answer: The customer's reaction works through the purchase, because that is the resource the customer supplies. A dissatisfied customer buys less often, buys a cheaper line, or moves to a competitor, and each of those shows up directly as lower revenue. Where the customer talks - to other buyers, or publicly - the same reaction reaches customers who have had no bad experience themselves, so the revenue effect spreads beyond the party that reacted. The business then either accepts the lower volume or spends money to recover it, through discounts, replacement or extra promotion, so the reaction lands on the results either as revenue lost or as cost incurred. How large that effect is depends on whether the customer has a close substitute available: where switching is easy the reaction arrives quickly as lost sales, and where it is not it arrives slowly as eroded goodwill.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must trace how the reaction travels - through the purchase, and through what the customer tells others.
The effect must land on revenue or on cost, because a reaction that does not reach the results has not been traced.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of predicting a stakeholder's reaction from the size of the effect on it alone.
items.canonical_answer: Size of effect is only one of the three things that drive a reaction, so using it alone overstates some reactions and misses others. A party badly affected but with no alternative and no way of organising may do almost nothing, because it has no lever: a customer in a settlement with one shop is hurt by a price rise and still buys. A party barely affected but highly organised or protected by law may react hard, because it can: a regulator inconvenienced by a minor breach can suspend a licence. The limitation matters because it leads a business to prepare for the wrong reaction - bracing for the loudest complaint so that the quiet party with real power is left unmanaged.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed, not stated: it must say what goes wrong because size of effect is used alone.
Both directions are required - a large effect with no lever, and a small effect with a strong lever.
Credit the practical consequence, which is that the business prepares for the wrong reaction.

items.prompt: Analyse how the aims of a business's largest customer come to shape the prices it sets.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that makes the aim count: the customer takes a large share of output, so the business depends on it and cannot replace the volume quickly. The customer's aim is a shelf price its own buyers accept, which means it wants the supply price held down. The mechanism by which that aim reaches the business is the purchase and the contract behind it - the customer can put the next order out to tender, delay renewal, or ask for a rebate, and each of those is a threat the business has to take seriously in proportion to the volume at risk. The business therefore prices with that account in mind: it holds or stages the increase for the large customer while taking more of it from smaller buyers who cannot apply the same pressure. The consequence is a price list that is no longer uniform, and an average realised price below the published one. The effect on the business's objectives is a thinner margin on its largest volume, which protects revenue and turnover while making the profit objective harder to reach - and the dependence deepens, because each year the account is retained on price the business becomes less able to walk away from it.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must open on the condition that gives the aim force - the share of output the customer takes.
Mechanism: the answer must say how the aim is transmitted, through tendering, renewal or rebate.
Consequence: a measurable result is required, such as a realised price below the published list.
Objective: the chain must finish on an effect on the business, and should note that the dependence itself deepens.

items.prompt: Swakop Seafoods is deciding whether to raise the price of frozen hake from N$78 to N$86 a pack. Its owners want a better return; its employees want secure shifts; its largest retail customer, which takes a third of output, wants shelf prices its shoppers accept. Explain whose aims are most likely to shape the decision.
items.canonical_answer: The retail customer's. The margin on each pack widens by N$86 - N$78 = N$8, which is what makes the rise attractive to the owners, and their pressure is real but indirect - the vote and the power to replace a director. The employees' aim for secure shifts is served by a stronger margin and threatened by lost volume, and their pressure, the willingness to work, is slow to apply. The retail customer's aim is backed by the most immediate pressure available: it can simply stop buying, and a third of output would then have to be sold elsewhere at short notice into a market that has just been told prices are rising. Weight follows dependence rather than merit, so the likely decision is a smaller or staged rise for that account with the full rise applied to the independent trade.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the named facts - the price move from N$78 to N$86 and the third of output taken by one customer.
Reasoning: the link must be that weight follows the pressure a party can apply, which follows dependence.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude with the shape of the decision that results, not only with a name.

items.prompt: A private limited company must choose between the pay settlement its employees are pressing for and the dividend its owners expect. Evaluate whether the aims of the stakeholder with the most influence should decide the outcome.
items.canonical_answer: No - influence should be read as information about what the decision will cost, not treated as the reason for it. The decisive criterion is which choice does more for the business's ability to keep trading: whether the pay settlement buys enough retention, effort and industrial peace to be worth its cost, set against what cutting the dividend does to the owners' willingness to leave capital in and to support the next request for funds. Influence enters that calculation because a party with real pressure can impose costs if its aim is refused - a strike costs output, a withdrawn shareholder costs future finance - so the pressure is part of the price of each option. In this company the employees' aim has the more immediate pressure behind it and the owners' the more durable, which is exactly why deciding by influence alone would favour the short term. The strongest argument for simply following influence is practical: a decision the most powerful party will not accept may not survive contact with reality, and managers who ignore that repeatedly lose the ability to act at all. On balance the aims of the most influential party should shape the decision without settling it, and the answer changes where the powerful party's aim happens to coincide with the business's own survival - a lender insisting on repayment, for instance - because then following influence and following the business's interest are the same course.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear position is required - influence informs the decision without settling it.
Context: the argument must be made for this company's own choice between a pay settlement and a dividend.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the effect on the business's ability to keep trading, with influence priced as a cost of refusal.
Counterargument: the practical case for following the most powerful party must be given real weight.
Condition: the answer must name what changes the judgement, such as the powerful party's aim coinciding with survival.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a stakeholder aim that becomes an objective of the business and one that becomes a constraint on it.
items.canonical_answer: An aim that becomes an objective is something the business has chosen to pursue and can weigh against its other objectives - a pay settlement it has committed to, a delivery standard it has published. An aim that becomes a constraint is a limit it has to work within whatever else it wants - an emissions ceiling set by a regulator, a condition attached to its borrowing. The distinction is in whether the aim can be traded off. An objective can be met more or less fully as circumstances change; a constraint either holds or is breached, and breaching it brings a consequence from outside the business - a penalty, a withdrawn licence, a facility called in. Identifying which kind an aim has become tells you whether the business still has a choice about it.
marking_guidance: Boundary: the distinction is whether the aim can be traded off against other objectives.
Both sides must be illustrated with a plausible example.
Credit the consequence: a breached constraint brings an external penalty, whereas a missed objective does not.

items.prompt: Explain why a business might choose to be accountable to its stakeholders beyond what the law requires.
items.canonical_answer: Because the parties it depends on commit their labour, custom, credit and goods on the strength of what they can find out about it. Where a business tells them little, they tend to protect themselves against what they cannot see - asking a higher price, offering shorter payment terms, seeking security over assets, or dealing with someone else - and each of those raises the cost of the resources the business needs. Voluntary disclosure lowers that cost by making the business's position checkable. A second reason is timing: reporting honestly to employees that the order book is falling brings the argument about hours forward to a point where short time is still an option, rather than leaving it until redundancy is the only remaining move.
marking_guidance: Reason: the answer must connect disclosure to the price at which the business obtains labour, custom, credit or goods.
Purpose: a second reason such as surfacing disagreement early strengthens the answer but one developed reason is sufficient.

items.prompt: Analyse how withholding information from its suppliers and its bank affects the terms on which a business can trade.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the position the withholding creates: the supplier and the bank each have money at risk in the business and no current picture of whether it can pay. Neither can distinguish a firm that is trading well from one that is not, so both price for the worse case, which is how the mechanism works - uncertainty is priced, not ignored. The supplier responds by shortening credit or asking for payment in advance; the bank responds by charging a higher rate, asking for security, or reducing the facility. The consequence is measurable: the business pays for goods sooner and for finance more dearly, so more cash is tied up in working capital at the same time as less is available. The effect on the business is a tighter cash position, which constrains the very trading it was trying to protect by saying nothing, and in a weak month can force it to turn down orders it could otherwise fund.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must begin from the condition - money at risk and no current information.
Mechanism: the answer must explain that uncertainty is priced, because the parties cannot distinguish a sound business from an unsound one.
Consequence: a measurable result is required - shorter credit, dearer finance, more cash tied up.
Objective: the chain must end on the effect on the business, which is a tighter cash position constraining trade.

items.prompt: A private limited company with fifteen employees is considering publishing an annual report on its environmental effects, as listed companies in its industry do. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer: It should not publish a full report of that kind, but it should disclose selectively to the parties that act on the information. The decisive criterion is whether the disclosure changes a decision by somebody the business depends on, because that is what makes reporting pay for itself rather than merely look responsible. For a listed company the answer is usually yes: the market prices what it can verify, and the reporting is required in any case. For a firm of fifteen the parties that matter are a handful of customers, a bank and a local community, and the cost of a full report - measurement, assurance, staff time - is carried by fifteen people's output rather than by a large revenue base. The strongest case for publishing is that its large customers may be under environmental reporting obligations of their own and may need data from their suppliers to meet them, in which case the report buys the contract and the calculation reverses. The judgement is therefore to disclose what specific customers ask for and to publish a short public statement for the local community, rather than to copy a listed company's format. That changes if the company intends to list or to seek external investment, because then it needs a reporting record before it is asked for one.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear recommendation is required, and a qualified one is acceptable provided the qualification is stated.
Context: the argument must use this business's facts - fifteen employees, private ownership, an industry where listed firms report.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether disclosure changes a decision by a party the business depends on.
Counterargument: the case that customers' own reporting obligations may require the data must be given real weight.
Condition: the answer must name what reverses it, such as an intention to list or to raise outside investment.

items.prompt: Katutura Tailors is a sole trader with three employees. Explain how the parties it must account to differ from those a public limited company in the same trade must account to.
items.canonical_answer: The tailor accounts mainly to the parties it has contracted with and to the tax authority: its three employees under their contracts and employment legislation, its customers under the terms of sale, its suppliers under the terms of purchase, and the revenue authority through its tax return. There is no outside owner to report to, because the owner runs the business, and no public filing of results. A public limited company in the same trade carries all of those and adds shareholders who take no part in running it, so it must publish audited accounts and an annual report, hold a general meeting, and disclose to the market on a timetable set by company law rather than by itself. The difference therefore follows the ownership form: separating ownership from control creates a body of people entitled to an account they cannot obtain by walking into the workshop.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must be built on this business's facts - a sole trader with three employees compared with a listed company in the same trade.
Reasoning: the link must be that separating ownership from control is what creates the additional reporting duty.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude that the difference follows the ownership form.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism that produces conflict between stakeholders even where each party is behaving reasonably.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is the finiteness of the business's money and capacity. N$1 of profit can be paid out as dividend, paid as higher wages, given away in a lower price, or reinvested in cleaner equipment - but once, not four times. Each of those uses serves a different party, so a decision that meets one party's aim necessarily reduces what is left for the others. No bad faith is needed anywhere in that sequence: the owner asking for a dividend and the employee asking for a rise are each asking for something defensible, and the conflict comes from the arithmetic of a shared pool rather than from the merits of either request. That is why conflict intensifies when the pool shrinks, and eases when it grows.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must locate the cause in the finite pool of money and capacity, not in bad faith.
Credit the consequence that conflict intensifies as the pool shrinks, because that shows the mechanism has been understood.

items.prompt: Otjiwarongo Charcoal has N$3 million of retained profit and three calls on it: a pay rise its workers are asking for, a price cut its largest customer wants, and dust-control equipment the neighbouring households want. Analyse how conflict between its stakeholders arises from this position.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that the N$3 million can fund one of the three claims fully, or parts of each, but not all three. That is what turns three reasonable requests into a conflict: the workers' aim of higher pay, the customer's aim of a lower price and the households' aim of less dust are each met out of the same pool, so meeting one reduces what remains for the others. The mechanism that sharpens it here is the mix of claimants. The workers and the customer both have contracts and can apply pressure - withdrawing labour, moving the account - so the business can bargain with them and can trade a smaller rise now against a larger one later. The households have no contract with the business and nothing to withhold, so there is no bargain to strike with them and their claim has nowhere to settle inside the business. The consequence is that spending is likely to go where pressure is, and the dust claim is likely to be deferred. The effect on the business is that the deferred claim does not disappear: it moves to the regional authority and the press, where it returns later as a permit condition or a compliance order, at a cost the business no longer controls.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must open on the condition - one pool of N$3 million against three claims on it.
Mechanism: the answer must explain why the claimants are not equivalent, because contract and pressure differ between them.
Consequence: a measurable result is required, such as the dust claim being deferred while the contracted claims are met.
Objective: the chain must end on the effect on the business, which is the deferred claim returning through the regulator at a cost it no longer controls.

items.prompt: Windhoek Wire Works is considering paying its suppliers in sixty days instead of thirty, to hold more cash through a slow quarter. Explain which stakeholders' aims conflict here and which do not.
items.canonical_answer: The conflict is between the suppliers and the owners. Suppliers want payment in thirty days because their own cash position depends on it; the owners want the cash held in the business through the slow quarter, and the same money cannot be in both places, so meeting one aim measurably reduces the other. The bank's aim and the owners' aim do not conflict here - a stronger cash position through a weak quarter lowers the risk of default, which is what the bank wants, so both are served by the same decision. The employees' aim does not conflict either, at least in the short run, because cash retained is what funds the payroll in a slow quarter. The conclusion is that this is a narrower conflict than it first appears: one relationship is being traded for the stability of the rest, which is why the answer turns on whether the suppliers can absorb sixty days without restricting future deliveries.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use this firm's facts - the move from thirty to sixty days through a slow quarter.
Reasoning: the link must distinguish aims that compete for the same money from aims that are served by the same decision.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude with the narrowness of the conflict and what the decision then turns on.

items.prompt: Evaluate the view that conflict between a business's stakeholders cannot be avoided.
items.canonical_answer: The view is largely right about the source of conflict and wrong about its inevitability in any particular decision. The decisive criterion is whether the resource in question is being divided or enlarged. Where it is divided - this year's profit split between dividend, wages, price and investment - conflict follows from arithmetic rather than from ill will, and no amount of consultation removes it. Where it is enlarged, aims turn out to be complementary: training that lifts product quality raises the employee's earning power, serves the customer and protects the owner's margin at once, so all three parties are better off from the same spending. A business that looks for those cases finds more of them than one that assumes every difference is a fight. The strongest argument for the view is timing: complementary decisions usually pay back later, while the division of this year's profit has to be settled now, so a business under pressure faces the dividing kind more often than the enlarging kind. The judgement is that conflict is structural rather than universal - it is built into any decision that splits a fixed pool, and avoidable in decisions that grow one. That shifts where the business is close to its cash limit, because a firm with no spare funds cannot take the enlarging option even when it can see it.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a definite position is required, and it must distinguish structural from universal.
Context: the answer must argue from business decisions of both kinds rather than in the abstract, naming at least one dividing and one enlarging decision.
Criterion: the decisive test must be whether the resource is being divided or enlarged.
Counterargument: the timing argument - that dividing decisions are immediate and enlarging ones pay back later - must be given real weight.
Condition: the answer must say what changes the judgement, such as a business at its cash limit being unable to take the enlarging option.

items.prompt: Correct this statement: "Wherever two stakeholders want different things, they are in conflict."
items.canonical_answer: Wanting different things is not the same as wanting incompatible things. Aims conflict where meeting one measurably reduces how far the other can be met, which happens when both are met out of the same limited pool. Aims are complementary where meeting one helps the other: a customer wanting more reliable delivery and an employee wanting better equipment want different things, and buying the equipment serves both. The corrected version: stakeholders are in conflict where their aims compete for the same limited resource, and not merely because the aims are different. The test to apply is whether the resource in question is being divided or enlarged.
marking_guidance: The error to be named is the assumption that difference implies incompatibility.
A corrected version of the statement is required.
An example of complementary aims supports the correction.

items.prompt: Analyse how a private limited company's move from distributing its profit to financing growth affects its owners, its employees and its suppliers.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is that the profit is now retained rather than paid out, so the same money changes destination. For the owners the immediate effect is a smaller dividend; the mechanism by which they may gain instead is that the retained money buys capacity, which raises future trading and the value of the shares, so what they receive is deferred rather than removed. Whether that is a gain to a particular owner depends on how long they intend to hold the shares, which is why a retiring shareholder and a young one can reasonably disagree about the same decision. For suppliers the effect runs the other way and arrives sooner: more capacity means larger and steadier orders, which lets them plan production and may earn the company better terms. For employees the effect is mixed - growth opens promotion routes and new roles, and it also brings more change, more training and often longer hours during the expansion. The consequence for the business is that its own risk rises, because growth financed partly by borrowing creates repayments that have to be met out of trading that has not happened yet. The effect on its objectives is therefore a trade of near-term certainty for a larger business later, and the trade is worth making only where the extra capacity is actually sold.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the chain must open on the condition - profit retained rather than distributed.
Mechanism: the answer must explain how retained money reaches each party, through capacity and orders.
Consequence: measurable effects are required for all three parties named in the question.
Objective: the chain must end on the effect on the business, including the rise in risk where growth is financed by borrowing.

items.prompt: Rundu Furniture's order book has fallen by a third and the board has moved from a growth objective to survival. Explain which of its stakeholders is likely to feel the change first, and why.
items.canonical_answer: Its employees, followed closely by its suppliers. A survival objective is pursued by cutting the outflows the business can change quickest, and in a workshop business the two quickest are hours worked and orders placed. With a third of the order book gone, short time or lay-offs can be introduced within a pay cycle, and orders to timber and fittings suppliers can be cut or delayed immediately. Owners feel the change as a suspended dividend, but that is decided at the year end, so it arrives months later. Customers may not feel it at all in the first quarter, since the firm has spare capacity and every reason to keep the remaining orders delivered on time. The conclusion is that the change lands first on whoever the business pays most frequently, which is why employees and suppliers carry the early cost of a survival objective.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the facts given - a third of the order book gone and a shift to survival.
Reasoning: the link must be the speed at which each outflow can be changed, not who is most important to the business.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude that the change lands first on the parties paid most frequently.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a manufacturer that adopts an environmental objective leaves its stakeholders better off overall.
items.canonical_answer: Not overall, and not evenly - the change redistributes before it improves anything, and whether it improves matters at all depends on conditions outside the manufacturer's control. The decisive criterion is whether the market or the regulator returns the cost. Cleaner equipment, certified inputs and better-controlled processes raise costs first, so in the short term the owners carry a lower return while the local community gains cleaner air and water sooner, and employees gain safer conditions. Whether the owners are compensated turns on two things: whether enough customers pay more for the cleaner product, and whether regulation makes competitors meet the same standard, which stops the manufacturer being undercut for doing it. Where both hold, the change is close to a general gain; where neither does, it is a transfer from owners to the community, defensible on other grounds but not a gain to everyone. The strongest argument for the general claim is that costs avoided later - fines, clean-up orders, the loss of customers who audit their supply chains - are real even though they are hard to date, so the comparison should not be made against this year's profit alone. The judgement is that stakeholders are not uniformly better off, and that the answer for the owners in particular hinges on customer willingness to pay and on whether the standard is imposed across the industry.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear position is required - the change redistributes and does not uniformly improve.
Context: the argument must be made about a manufacturer's own costs, customers and community rather than in general terms.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether the market or the regulator returns the cost to the owners.
Counterargument: the case that avoided future costs make the change pay must be given real weight.
Condition: the answer must name the conditions that change it - customers paying more, or regulation binding competitors.

items.prompt: Explain the difference, for a business's employees, between a move to a growth objective and a move to a survival objective.
items.canonical_answer: Under a move to growth the business spends more on capacity, so employees face more work, more training and more change, and gain new roles and promotion routes as the business gets bigger; the pressure on them comes from expansion. Under a move to survival the business cuts the outflows it can change quickest, and wages are among them, so employees face reduced hours, lay-offs or a pay freeze; the pressure comes from contraction. The distinction worth holding is in direction and speed. Growth affects employees gradually and mostly enlarges what is available to them, whereas survival affects them within a pay cycle and reduces it, because hours are one of the few costs a business can change quickly.
marking_guidance: Boundary: the difference is between expansion and contraction, in both direction and speed of effect.
Both sides must be described, with at least one concrete effect on employees each.
Credit the point that hours can be changed quickly, which is why survival reaches employees first.

items.prompt: Explain the mechanism by which a business's move to a survival objective reaches its suppliers.
items.canonical_answer: A survival objective means preserving cash, and the two levers a business can pull quickly are what it pays out and when. Both bear on suppliers. It reduces orders, because holding less stock releases cash tied up in it, so the supplier's volume falls. It also stretches payment, taking sixty days where the agreement says thirty, so the supplier finances the business for longer and its own cash position tightens in turn. The mechanism is therefore a transfer of the cash-flow problem down the chain, and it reaches the supplier faster than a dividend cut reaches the owners, because order and payment decisions are taken weekly while distributions are decided once a year. A supplier that cannot absorb it may respond by shortening terms or giving priority to other buyers, which returns the pressure to the business.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: the answer must trace both levers - reduced orders and stretched payment - and say how each reaches the supplier.
Credit the return effect, because a supplier that tightens its own terms sends the pressure back.

items.prompt: Zambezi River Lodge employs 34 people, buys produce from four growers within 20 km, and sits beside a village of about 500 on communal land. For each of three named stakeholders of the lodge, identify whether it is internal or external, and explain the role that party plays in the lodge's activity.
items.canonical_answer: Its housekeeping and kitchen employees: internal, because they form part of the organisation. Role: they supply the labour and the service skill the guests are paying for. The four produce growers: external, because they are separate businesses dealing with the lodge under contracts of sale. Role: they supply the fresh inputs the kitchen works with, on agreed terms. The village: external, because it is not part of the organisation. Role: it hosts the operation on communal land and supplies most of the workforce, which is why its position is stronger than that of a neighbour who merely lives nearby.

items.prompt: Otjiwarongo Charcoal is deciding whether to move to a night shift to raise output by 40 per cent. Four stakeholder positions are on the record. Its 48 production workers, through a recognised union: willing to work nights only with a 25 per cent shift premium. Its largest customer, taking 55 per cent of output: has asked for the extra volume and has said it will look elsewhere for it if the volume is not available by March. The households nearest the kilns: have objected to night noise to the regional council, which is considering a night-operating condition on the licence. The two owners: want the extra volume, and calculate that the shift premium absorbs about half the margin on the additional output. Using this information, analyse how the decision affects each of these parties and evaluate whether the move should go ahead.
items.canonical_answer:
Analysis, party by party. The 48 workers gain paid hours and a 25 per cent premium, and lose evenings and sleep; their influence is high, because they are organised and no night shift runs without them. The customer gains the volume it has asked for; its influence is the highest of the four, because 55 per cent of output cannot be replaced quickly and it has named a date. The households lose amenity and have no contract with the business, so their route runs through the regional council - slower than the others, and capable of imposing a condition the business cannot negotiate away. The owners gain the additional margin, halved by the premium, and carry the risk if the licence condition arrives after the shift is staffed.

Evaluation. The move should go ahead, conditionally. The decisive criterion is whether the additional margin after the premium still exceeds the cost of the reactions, and here the premium is a known cost that leaves about half the additional margin, while the customer's departure is a much larger and more likely loss - 55 per cent of output moving elsewhere would cost far more than the premium on the extra 40 per cent. The strongest argument against is the licence condition: if the council restricts night operation after the shift is recruited, the business carries the premium and the recruitment cost without the volume, and it has no way of forcing that decision. The judgement is therefore to proceed, but to secure the noise position first - approaching the council before recruiting, and offering noise mitigation at the kilns - and to seek a volume commitment from the customer so that the additional capacity has somewhere to go. The judgement reverses where the council indicates it will impose a restriction, because the shift would then be committed against volume the business may not be allowed to produce.
marking_guidance: Judgement: an explicit recommendation is required, with its conditions stated.
Context: every part of the answer must use the figures given - 48 workers, a 25 per cent premium, 55 per cent of output, the March date, the licence application.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be the additional margin after the premium set against the cost of the reactions.
Counterargument: the licence risk must be treated as the strongest argument against, not mentioned in passing.
Condition: the answer must say what reverses the recommendation, namely an indication that the council will restrict night operation.
All four parties must be analysed before the judgement is reached.

facts: largest customer takes 55 per cent of output

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Rundu Furniture has grown for six years by retaining almost all of its profit. Its two owners, who are approaching retirement, now want the business to change its objective from growth to maximising the annual distribution. Its 60 employees, its timber suppliers and the bank that financed its last workshop extension are all affected. Evaluate whether the change of objective should be made.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: the change is defensible for the owners but should be phased rather than made at once, and the deciding factor is whether the business can meet its existing repayments while distributing more.

Paragraph 1 - what the change actually moves: profit that currently buys capacity would instead leave the business, so the pool every party draws on stops growing. Name the amounts at issue rather than describing the change in the abstract.

Paragraph 2 - who gains and who bears it: the owners gain income now, which matches their retirement horizon; suppliers face static or falling orders where capacity stops expanding; employees lose the promotion routes growth created, though their current jobs are not immediately at risk; the bank sees a business distributing cash rather than building the asset base that supports its lending.

Paragraph 3 - where the genuine conflict lies: not between owners and employees in general, but between the owners' timing and the bank's security. This is a dividing decision rather than an enlarging one, so it cannot be resolved by finding a shared gain.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest case for the change: the owners carried the risk for six years and took little out; a business that never distributes gives its owners no return at all, and retirement is a legitimate reason to convert years of retained profit into income.

Judgement and condition: phase the increase in distribution over three years so repayments stay covered and orders to suppliers do not fall abruptly; revisit if trading weakens, because a business under cash pressure that has committed to a larger distribution has to cut hours or orders to fund it. The judgement changes if the owners intend to sell rather than retire in place, because a buyer would value the reinvested capacity more than the distribution record.
marking_guidance: A plan rather than an essay: what is assessed is the structure and the stated judgement.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached and what it is.
Context: the plan must use this firm's facts - six years of retention, two owners near retirement, 60 employees, timber suppliers, a bank that financed the extension.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether repayments stay covered while more is distributed.
Counterargument: the owners' case for taking income after six years of retention must be argued, not dismissed.
Condition: the plan must end on what would change the answer, such as an intention to sell the business.

facts: bank financed the last workshop extension

items.prompt: Namib Clay Bricks has run a kiln beside a settlement for eleven years. Dust readings have risen since it added a second kiln. The company has not published the readings. Its 70 employees live in the settlement; its largest customer, a construction firm taking 45 per cent of output, has begun asking suppliers for environmental data; the regional council has received complaints and has asked the company for the readings; the two owners say that dust-control equipment would cost N$2 million, which is a full year's retained profit. Analyse the stakeholder position the company is in, and evaluate what it should do about disclosure.
items.canonical_answer:
Analysis. The company is holding information that four parties have a reason to want, and each has a different route to it. The council can require the readings and can attach conditions to the operating licence, so its route is legal and cannot be refused for long. The construction customer can require them as a condition of continued supply, and with 45 per cent of output at stake that request is close to binding. The employees live in the settlement, so they are on both sides of the dust question at once - the jobs and the exposure are theirs together - and they can act collectively at work. The settlement itself has no contract with the company and no data, so its route runs through the council or the press, which is slow but not weak, because it is the council that renews the licence.

The conflict is a dividing one. The N$2 million that would control the dust is a full year's retained profit, so spending it means the owners forgo a year's return; the same money cannot buy equipment and remain a distribution. Withholding the readings does not avoid that conflict, it defers it, and deferral has a cost of its own: parties that cannot verify a position tend to assume the worst, so the customer may requalify its supply and the council may set a tighter condition than the readings would have justified.

Evaluation. The company should disclose the readings, to the council and to the customer first and then publicly, and should commit to a dated programme for the equipment. The decisive criterion is that accountability here is not optional in substance: two parties can compel the information and a third can withdraw nearly half the revenue, so the real choice is between disclosing on its own terms now and disclosing on someone else's terms later. The strongest argument against is cash: N$2 million is a year's retained profit, disclosure will accelerate the demand for it, and a company that announces a problem it cannot yet fund invites a licence condition it cannot meet. That argument supports staging the spending rather than delaying the disclosure, because the customer and the council are asking about the readings, not about the equipment. The judgement changes where the readings turn out to be within the limits the licence sets, since publishing them would then settle the matter at no cost at all - which is a further reason to look at them before deciding.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a clear recommendation on disclosure is required, with its sequence stated.
Context: the answer must use the facts given - eleven years, a second kiln, 70 employees in the settlement, 45 per cent of output, N$2 million equal to a year's retained profit.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be that two parties can compel the information and a third can withdraw nearly half the revenue.
Counterargument: the cash argument against early disclosure must be argued properly before it is answered.
Condition: the answer must name what would change it, such as readings that turn out to be within the licence limits.
The analysis must cover all four parties and must identify the conflict as one over a divided sum.

context.situation: undisclosed dust readings beside a settlement
facts: largest customer takes 45 per cent of output
equal to one year of retained profit
